video_title: Black October, Banks vs. AI, Visa/Fireblocks? - The Chopping Block
gist: Dragonfly/Gauntlet/Superstate panel discusses the 'Black October' wave of 10/10 web CVEs driven by AI cyber capability, banks blocking AI agents, a rumored Visa-Fireblocks deal, and AI-infrastructure financing risk.

insights.claim: In roughly 48 hours multiple 10/10 CVEs were disclosed across core web infrastructure, including two PHP remote-code-execution flaws ('PHP 2 Shell') exploitable with one line, Node.js RCE flaws, Linux kernel exploits posted to a mailing list without responsible disclosure, a GitLab RCE, a Railway breach and a QUIC zero-day.
insights.speaker: Tom (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Cyber-incident clustering raises demand for patching, security tooling and auditors; watch exposed long-tail PHP/WordPress stacks.

insights.claim: Government sites are among the largest remaining PHP users, so Finland, the Netherlands, France and Japan took services offline or took over sites, and the NSA reportedly told operators to take web services down if they could not patch.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Public-sector legacy stacks are a systemic weak point; sovereign cyber response is now a market-moving category.

insights.claim: Microsoft reportedly caught a custom agent, attributed to a Chinese state-aligned actor, indexing and exploiting its security threat intelligence and the newly published CVEs in the wild.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Autonomous exploit agents shrink the time between disclosure and mass exploitation.

insights.claim: Despite being the worst batch of web vulnerabilities seen so far, the realized blast radius was contained: crypto fallout was mainly a Railway compromise that exposed a DeFi project's keys and let an attacker upgrade its contracts.
insights.speaker: Tom (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Scary headline severity has not yet translated into large losses; second-order effects remain unknown.
insights.quote: this is like the doomsday batch of security vulnerabilities, and not that much broke

insights.claim: The wave looks like the tip of the iceberg: AI cyber capability that was technically possible for 6-7 months with frontier models is now widely available, mirroring the 'oh no' moment coding agents had for SaaS, and low-hanging fruit gets hit before attacks get sophisticated.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Expect repeated vulnerability waves; security spend and audit capacity should keep rising.

insights.claim: Closed source is argued to be less safe than open source in the AI era because binaries can be reverse engineered easily and compromises of closed stacks can stay hidden for long periods, whereas open-source exploitation is disseminated quickly.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Counters the 'open source is dead because of AI' thesis; favors transparency-based security models.
insights.quote: sunlight is the best disinfectant in the long run

insights.claim: Crypto teams were ahead on live threat detection, sandboxing and security posture after dealing with exploits earlier this year, while SF software teams that dismissed such practices are now trying to buy crypto auditors.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Crypto security vendors and auditors may find demand from mainstream software.

insights.claim: During the incident, major closed labs refused or slowed help with emergency patching and secret rotation (OpenAI via its Daybreak sign-up, Anthropic via slow Mythos/security access), so open-weight models were the only reliable option for live defense.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Liability-driven refusals create a structural niche for open-weight models in high-reliability tasks.

insights.claim: Anywhere closed model providers' liability concerns block use (cybersecurity, trading), open models win; AI trading agents did not take off until open models caught up, a split that resembles crypto's.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Look for open-model and local-agent adoption in finance and security use cases.

insights.claim: Large banks and brokers are restricting AI agents that users give credentials to: JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, Citi, Wells Fargo and Schwab (which blocked Muse) cite unauthorized activity, and some now block even read-only access.
insights.speaker: Rob (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Incumbent friction toward agents is rising; track which banks and brokers choose to enable agents.

insights.claim: The 'agentic bank run' fear (Apollo's Torsten Slok on agents sweeping cash out of low-yield checking) is overdone, and the real bank motive is protecting roughly $1.6 trillion of non-interest-bearing deposits and lock-in via deliberate friction.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Agents that lower switching costs threaten bank deposit margins; banks that enable them may gain.

insights.claim: Banks took about a decade to accept read-only Plaid access, so an agent that can click buttons is seen as an order of magnitude scarier; claims of agents acting beyond user instructions are viewed as hyperbole.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Expect slow, defensive bank adoption; the pattern follows Plaid's history.

insights.claim: Blocking will be only partly effective: banks and sites cannot tell local agents (e.g. Hermes) from the user, and open-source tooling improves in UX over time. A counterpoint holds that few people will run local agents, so volume is de minimis near term.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Distribution depends on UX; hosted-agent vendors face blocking while local agents are hard to stop.

insights.claim: Asset managers can block agents much more easily than banks because they have no demand-deposit withdrawal guarantee, while banks cannot reliably distinguish a user from software acting for them.
insights.speaker: Tom (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Friction-based defenses differ by business model; banks are more exposed.

insights.claim: Health insurers are the clearest losers if AI agents navigate paperwork on consumers' behalf, and are the industry one speaker would most want to short.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Possible short thesis on incumbents whose profits depend on consumer navigation friction.
insights.quote: If there's any industry I would want to short, that's what I would want to short.

insights.claim: Progressive politicians such as Bernie Sanders calling to pause AI over agents in bank accounts are criticized as taking the banks' side against consumers; liability and consumer-protection debate around AI is growing in DC.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk for consumer-facing agents is rising despite consumer-surplus benefits.

insights.claim: Joe Weisenthal's 'blockchain not Bitcoin' reversal after interviewing Hyperliquid's founder is read as TradFi converging on perps as a substrate for equities, commodities and pre-IPO markets, with oil trading on the Iran war weekend and the Cerebras IPO as proof moments.
insights.speaker: Tom (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Perp DEXs are proving a case for 24/7 markets in non-crypto assets.

insights.claim: CME's Terry Duffy remains the leading critic of perps and prediction markets, arguing for guardrails; the panel jokes about onion-futures advocates and sees the regulatory fight continuing.
insights.speaker: Rob (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Incumbent exchange opposition is a regulatory headwind for perps and prediction markets.

insights.claim: The panel sees everything in market structure and commerce drifting to look like crypto (anonymous agent swarms, sybil risk), and so winners and losers in agent commerce should resemble those in crypto.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Crypto primitives (identity, payments, stablecoins) are relevant to agent commerce.

insights.claim: Axios reported Visa may buy Fireblocks for about $2-2.5 billion, which Fireblocks denied; Fireblocks last raised at $8 billion in 2021 and the deal would be Visa's first acquisition in the space.
insights.speaker: Rob (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Strategic acquirers are a likelier exit than IPOs for crypto infrastructure; watch Visa's stablecoin plans.

insights.claim: A sale below the 2021 peak would still be a fine outcome: the wallet market is sideways, crypto IPO appetite is thin next to OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX, and 2021 round prices were bubble prices (blockchain.com $13B, Chainalysis $8B, Alchemy $10B, OpenSea $13B).
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Expect further M&A and down-rounds among 2021-vintage crypto companies; crypto is becoming 'finance plus plus'.

insights.claim: Character AI filed for bankruptcy after raising at $2.5 billion from Andreessen while burning about $16 of compute for every $1 of revenue, which suggests many AI companies may have similarly poor unit economics.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Watch AI app-layer failures if VC funding slows.

insights.claim: A duration mismatch in AI infrastructure could trigger a financial crisis: neoclouds and hyperscalers fund with roughly 10-year debt but sell 1-5 year contracts onward to inference providers, who resell quarterly, and the yields do not add up.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Credit stress in AI infrastructure would show first in neocloud debt; monitor refinancing and contract renewals.
insights.quote: there's a lot of duration mismatch here

insights.claim: CoreWeave's roughly 15% debt is only the unsecured piece, most debt is secured against future contracts, and Nvidia's equity backstop puts it ahead of other neoclouds, so the market may be irrationally punishing it.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Relative-value view: CoreWeave versus weaker neoclouds.
